justification_text:
My point estimates were anchored primarily to the prevailing price level at the time of the forecast, with relatively modest drift assumed across all three horizons. For the one-day estimate, I expected price to stay close to its recent trading range, reflecting the tendency for asset prices to exhibit mean-reversion or continuity over very short periods absent a major catalyst. The one-week and one-month estimates nudged slightly higher, reflecting a mild upward bias that could come from broader market momentum or a slight structural drift, but the adjustments were small because I lacked strong conviction in a directional move over those periods. Essentially, the forecast treated the current level as the best starting anchor and applied only modest adjustments for trend.

The confidence interval widths were calibrated to reflect how uncertainty compounds over time. Over a single day, the range is relatively tight because there are few hours for new information to accumulate and because intraday volatility, while real, tends to be bounded within a session. By one week, a wider band is warranted because several trading sessions can each introduce independent shocks, earnings announcements, economic data releases, or shifts in sentiment. Over one month, the interval widens further still because macroeconomic developments, central bank communications, geopolitical events, and sector-specific news can all materialize and interact in ways that are difficult to anticipate. The asymmetry in interval width across horizons is essentially a reflection of the square-root-of-time scaling of volatility under standard diffusion assumptions.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside the stated intervals include a sudden and large macroeconomic shock, such as an unexpected inflation print, an emergency central bank action, or a geopolitical escalation that triggers broad risk-off selling. On the upside, a surprise positive catalyst — such as a strong earnings beat, a policy announcement favorable to the sector, or a short-squeeze dynamic — could propel prices well above the upper bound of the one-month interval. Liquidity conditions also matter; if market depth thins during a holiday period or following a large institutional rebalancing, price movements can be more extreme than historical volatility would suggest. These tail events are precisely what standard confidence intervals tend to underweight, so readers should treat the outer bounds as indicative rather than exhaustive.
